title: Cell-free fetal DNA
wikitext:
{{short description|Fetal DNA in the maternal bloodstream}}
'''Cell-free fetal DNA''' ('''cffDNA''') is [[fetal]] [[DNA]] that [[Circulating free DNA|circulates freely]] in the maternal [[blood]]. Maternal blood is sampled by [[venipuncture]]. Analysis of cffDNA is a method of [[Prenatal diagnosis#By invasiveness|non-invasive prenatal diagnosis]] frequently ordered for [[Advanced maternal age|pregnant women of advanced age]]. Two hours after delivery, cffDNA is no longer detectable in maternal blood.

==Background==
[[File:Cell free fetal DNA shedding into maternal bloodstream.pdf|thumb|Cell-free fetal DNA sheds into the maternal blood circulation.]]
cffDNA originates from [[placenta]]l [[trophoblast]]s.<ref name=Alberry2007>{{cite journal | vauthors = Alberry M, Maddocks D, Jones M, Abdel Hadi M, Abdel-Fattah S, Avent N, Soothill PW | title = Free fetal DNA in maternal plasma in anembryonic pregnancies: confirmation that the origin is the trophoblast | journal = Prenatal Diagnosis | volume = 27 | issue = 5 | pages = 415–8 | date = May 2007 | pmid = 17286310 | doi = 10.1002/pd.1700 | publisher = Wiley-Blackwell | s2cid = 39693586 }}</ref><ref name=Gupta2004>{{cite journal | vauthors = Gupta AK, Holzgreve W, Huppertz B, Malek A, Schneider H, Hahn S | title = Detection of fetal DNA and RNA in placenta-derived syncytiotrophoblast microparticles generated in vitro | journal = Clinical Chemistry | volume = 50 | issue = 11 | pages = 2187–90 | date = November 2004 | pmid = 15502097 | doi = 10.1373/clinchem.2004.040196 | publisher = American Association for Clinical Chemistry (AACC) | doi-access = free }}</ref> Fetal DNA is fragmented when placental microparticles are shed into the maternal blood [[circulatory system|circulation]].<ref name=SmetsVisser2006>{{cite journal | vauthors = Smets EM, Visser A, Go AT, van Vugt JM, Oudejans CB | title = Novel biomarkers in preeclampsia | journal = Clinica Chimica Acta; International Journal of Clinical Chemistry | volume = 364 | issue = 1–2 | pages = 22–32 | date = February 2006 | pmid = 16139262 | doi = 10.1016/j.cca.2005.06.011 | publisher = Elsevier BV }}</ref>

cffDNA fragments are approximately 200 base pairs (bp) in length. They are significantly smaller than [[Circulating free DNA|maternal DNA fragments]].<ref name=Chan2004>{{cite journal | vauthors = Chan KC, Zhang J, Hui AB, Wong N, Lau TK, Leung TN, Lo KW, Huang DW, Lo YM | title = Size distributions of maternal and fetal DNA in maternal plasma | journal = Clinical Chemistry | volume = 50 | issue = 1 | pages = 88–92 | date = January 2004 | pmid = 14709639 | doi = 10.1373/clinchem.2003.024893 | publisher = American Association for Clinical Chemistry (AACC) | doi-access = free }}</ref> The difference in size allows cffDNA to be distinguished from maternal DNA fragments.<ref name=Li2004>{{cite journal | vauthors = Li Y, Zimmermann B, Rusterholz C, Kang A, Holzgreve W, Hahn S | title = Size separation of circulatory DNA in maternal plasma permits ready detection of fetal DNA polymorphisms | journal = Clinical Chemistry | volume = 50 | issue = 6 | pages = 1002–11 | date = June 2004 | pmid = 15073090 | doi = 10.1373/clinchem.2003.029835 | url = http://clinchem.aaccjnls.org/content/clinchem/50/6/1002.full.pdf | publisher = American Association for Clinical Chemistry (AACC) | doi-access = free }}</ref><ref name=Li2005>{{cite journal | vauthors = Li Y, Di Naro E, Vitucci A, Zimmermann B, Holzgreve W, Hahn S | title = Detection of paternally inherited fetal point mutations for beta-thalassemia using size-fractionated cell-free DNA in maternal plasma | journal = JAMA | volume = 293 | issue = 7 | pages = 843–9 | date = February 2005 | pmid = 15713774 | doi = 10.1001/jama.293.7.843 | publisher = American Medical Association (AMA) | doi-access = free }}</ref>

Approximately 11 to 13.4 percent of the cell-free DNA in maternal blood is of fetal origin. The amount varies widely from one pregnant woman to another.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Wang E, Batey A, Struble C, Musci T, Song K, Oliphant A | s2cid = 31630351 | title = Gestational age and maternal weight effects on fetal cell-free DNA in maternal plasma | journal = Prenatal Diagnosis | volume = 33 | issue = 7 | pages = 662–6 | date = July 2013 | pmid = 23553731 | doi = 10.1002/pd.4119 | doi-access = free }}</ref> cffDNA is present after five to seven weeks gestation. The amount of cffDNA increases as the pregnancy progresses.<ref name=Lo1998b>{{cite journal | vauthors = Lo YM, Tein MS, Lau TK, Haines CJ, Leung TN, Poon PM, Wainscoat JS, Johnson PJ, Chang AM, Hjelm NM | title = Quantitative analysis of fetal DNA in maternal plasma and serum: implications for noninvasive prenatal diagnosis | journal = American Journal of Human Genetics | volume = 62 | issue = 4 | pages = 768–75 | date = April 1998 | pmid = 9529358 | pmc = 1377040 | doi = 10.1086/301800 | publisher = Elsevier BV }}</ref> The quantity of cffDNA in maternal blood diminishes rapidly after childbirth. Two hours after delivery, cffDNA is no longer detectable in maternal blood.<ref name=Lo1999a>{{cite journal | vauthors = Lo YM, Zhang J, Leung TN, Lau TK, Chang AM, Hjelm NM | title = Rapid clearance of fetal DNA from maternal plasma | journal = American Journal of Human Genetics | volume = 64 | issue = 1 | pages = 218–24 | date = January 1999 | pmid = 9915961 | pmc = 1377720 | doi = 10.1086/302205 | publisher = Elsevier BV }}</ref>

Analysis of cffDNA may provide earlier diagnosis of fetal conditions than current techniques. As cffDNA is found in maternal blood, sampling carries no associated risk of [[spontaneous abortion]].<ref name=Lo1998a>{{cite journal | vauthors = Lo YM, Hjelm NM, Fidler C, Sargent IL, Murphy MF, Chamberlain PF, Poon PM, Redman CW, Wainscoat JS | title = Prenatal diagnosis of fetal RhD status by molecular analysis of maternal plasma | journal = The New England Journal of Medicine | volume = 339 | issue = 24 | pages = 1734–8 | date = December 1998 | pmid = 9845707 | doi = 10.1056/nejm199812103392402 | publisher = New England Journal of Medicine (NEJM/MMS) | doi-access = free }}</ref><ref name=AllyseSayres2012>{{cite journal | vauthors = Allyse M, Sayres LC, King JS, Norton ME, Cho MK | title = Cell-free fetal DNA testing for fetal aneuploidy and beyond: clinical integration challenges in the US context | journal = Human Reproduction | volume = 27 | issue = 11 | pages = 3123–31 | date = November 2012 | pmid = 22863603 | pmc = 3472618 | doi = 10.1093/humrep/des286 | publisher = Oxford University Press (OUP) }}</ref><ref name=MujezinovicAlfirevic2007>{{cite journal | vauthors = Mujezinovic F, Alfirevic Z | title = Procedure-related complications of amniocentesis and chorionic villous sampling: a systematic review | journal = Obstetrics and Gynecology | volume = 110 | issue = 3 | pages = 687–94 | date = September 2007 | pmid = 17766619 | doi = 10.1097/01.aog.0000278820.54029.e3 | publisher = Ovid Technologies (Wolters Kluwer Health) | s2cid = 25548568 }}</ref><ref name=Lo2008>{{cite journal | vauthors = Lo YM | s2cid = 3445205 | title = Fetal nucleic acids in maternal plasma | journal = Annals of the New York Academy of Sciences | volume = 1137 | issue = 1 | pages = 140–3 | date = August 2008 | pmid = 18837938 | doi = 10.1196/annals.1448.004 | publisher = Wiley-Blackwell | bibcode = 2008NYASA1137..140L }}</ref><ref name=nhs2016>{{cite web | url = http://www.rapid.nhs.uk/ | work = The NHS RAPID project | title = Reliable Accurate Prenatal non-Invasive Diagnosis | access-date = 2016-07-08 | archive-date = 2019-03-01 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20190301230057/http://www.rapid.nhs.uk/ }}</ref> cffDNA analysis has the same [[Prenatal diagnosis#Ethical and practical issues|ethical and practical issues]] as other techniques such as [[amniocentesis]] and [[chorionic villus sampling]].<ref name=HahnChitty2008/>

Some disadvantages of sampling cffDNA include a low concentration of cffDNA in maternal blood; variation in the quantity of cffDNA between individuals; a high concentration of maternal cell free DNA compared to the cffDNA in maternal blood.<ref name=WrightBurton2009>{{cite journal | vauthors = Wright CF, Burton H | title = The use of cell-free fetal nucleic acids in maternal blood for non-invasive prenatal diagnosis | journal = Human Reproduction Update | volume = 15 | issue = 1 | pages = 139–51 | date = 22 October 2008 | pmid = 18945714 | doi = 10.1093/humupd/dmn047 | publisher = Oxford University Press (OUP) | doi-access = free }}</ref>

New evidence shows that cffDNA test [[failure rate]] is higher, fetal fraction (proportion of fetal versus maternal DNA in the maternal blood sample) is lower and PPV for trisomies 18, 13 and SCA is decreased in IVF pregnancies compared to those conceived spontaneously.{{clarify|date=March 2024}}<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Lee TJ, Rolnik DL, Menezes MA, McLennan AC, da Silva Costa F | title = Cell-free fetal DNA testing in singleton IVF conceptions | journal = Human Reproduction | volume = 33 | issue = 4 | pages = 572–578 | date = April 2018 | pmid = 29462319 | doi = 10.1093/humrep/dey033 | doi-access = free | hdl = 10072/413913 | hdl-access = free }}</ref>

==Laboratory methods==

A number of laboratory methods have been developed for cell-free fetal DNA screening for genetic defects have been developed.  The main ones are (1) massively parallel [[shotgun sequencing]] (MPSS), (2) targeted massive parallel sequencing (t-MPS) and (3) [[single nucleotide polymorphism]] (SNP) based approach.<ref name="Dar_2016">{{cite journal | vauthors = Dar P, Shani H, Evans MI | title = Cell-free DNA: Comparison of Technologies | journal = Clinics in Laboratory Medicine | volume = 36 | issue = 2 | pages = 199–211 | date = June 2016 | pmid = 27235906 | doi = 10.1016/j.cll.2016.01.015 }}</ref><ref name="Grace_2016">{{cite journal | vauthors = Grace MR, Hardisty E, Dotters-Katz SK, Vora NL, Kuller JA | title = Cell-Free DNA Screening: Complexities and Challenges of Clinical Implementation | journal = Obstetrical & Gynecological Survey | volume = 71 | issue = 8 | pages = 477–87 | date = August 2016 | pmid = 27526871 | pmc = 5548289 | doi = 10.1097/OGX.0000000000000342 }}</ref><ref name="Allen_2017">{{cite journal | vauthors = Allen S, Young E, Bowns B | title = Noninvasive prenatal diagnosis for single gene disorders | journal = Current Opinion in Obstetrics & Gynecology | volume = 29 | issue = 2 | pages = 73–79 | date = April 2017 | pmid = 28134670 | doi = 10.1097/GCO.0000000000000347 | s2cid = 33474139 }}</ref>

A maternal peripheral blood sample is taken by [[venesection]] at about ten weeks gestation.<ref name=Guibert2003>{{cite journal | vauthors = Guibert J, Benachi A, Grebille AG, Ernault P, Zorn JR, Costa JM | title = Kinetics of SRY gene appearance in maternal serum: detection by real time PCR in early pregnancy after assisted reproductive technique | journal = Human Reproduction | volume = 18 | issue = 8 | pages = 1733–6 | date = August 2003 | pmid = 12871892 | doi = 10.1093/humrep/deg320 | doi-access = free }}</ref>

===Separation of cffDNA===
[[Blood plasma]] is separated from the maternal blood sample using a [[laboratory centrifuge]]. The cffDNA is then isolated and purified.<ref name=Chiu2001>{{cite journal | vauthors = Chiu RW, Poon LL, Lau TK, Leung TN, Wong EM, Lo YM | title = Effects of blood-processing protocols on fetal and total DNA quantification in maternal plasma | journal = Clinical Chemistry | volume = 47 | issue = 9 | pages = 1607–13 | date = September 2001 | pmid = 11514393 | doi = 10.1093/clinchem/47.9.1607 | doi-access = free }}</ref> A standardized protocol for doing this was written  through an evaluation of the [[scientific literature]]. The highest yield in cffDNA extraction was obtained with the "QIAamp DSP Virus Kit".<ref name=Legler2007>{{cite journal | vauthors = Legler TJ, Liu Z, Mavrou A, Finning K, Hromadnikova I, Galbiati S, Meaney C, Hultén MA, Crea F, Olsson ML, Maddocks DG, Huang D, Fisher SA, Sprenger-Haussels M, Soussan AA, van der Schoot CE | title = Workshop report on the extraction of foetal DNA from maternal plasma | journal = Prenatal Diagnosis | volume = 27 | issue = 9 | pages = 824–9 | date = September 2007 | pmid = 17604339 | doi = 10.1002/pd.1783 | publisher = Wiley-Blackwell | s2cid = 38860225 }}</ref>

Addition of [[formaldehyde]] to maternal blood samples increases the yield of cffDNA. Formaldehyde stabilizes intact cells, and therefore inhibits the further release of maternal DNA. With the addition of formaldehyde, the percentage of cffDNA recovered from a maternal blood sample varies between 0.32 percent and 40 percent with a mean of 7.7 percent.<ref name=Dhallan2004>{{cite journal | vauthors = Dhallan R, Au WC, Mattagajasingh S, Emche S, Bayliss P, Damewood M, Cronin M, Chou V, Mohr M | title = Methods to increase the percentage of free fetal DNA recovered from the maternal circulation | journal = JAMA | volume = 291 | issue = 9 | pages = 1114–9 | date = March 2004 | pmid = 14996781 | doi = 10.1001/jama.291.9.1114 | publisher = American Medical Association (AMA) | doi-access = free }}</ref> Without the addition of  formaldehyde, the mean percentage of cffDNA recovered has been measured at 20.2 percent. However, other figures vary between 5 and 96 percent.<ref name=Benachi2005>{{cite journal | vauthors = Benachi A, Yamgnane A, Olivi M, Dumez Y, Gautier E, Costa JM | title = Impact of formaldehyde on the in vitro proportion of fetal DNA in maternal plasma and serum | journal = Clinical Chemistry | volume = 51 | issue = 1 | pages = 242–4 | date = January 2005 | pmid = 15514098 | doi = 10.1373/clinchem.2004.038125 | publisher = American Association for Clinical Chemistry (AACC) | doi-access = free }}</ref><ref name=ChinnapapagariHolzgreve2005>{{cite journal | vauthors = Chinnapapagari SK, Holzgreve W, Lapaire O, Zimmermann B, Hahn S | title = Treatment of maternal blood samples with formaldehyde does not alter the proportion of circulatory fetal nucleic acids (DNA and mRNA) in maternal plasma | journal = Clinical Chemistry | volume = 51 | issue = 3 | pages = 652–5 | date = March 2005 | pmid = 15738521 | doi = 10.1373/clinchem.2004.042119 | publisher = American Association for Clinical Chemistry (AACC) | doi-access = free }}</ref>

Recovery of cffDNA may be related to the length of the DNA fragments. Another way to increase the fetal DNA is based on physical length of DNA fragments. Smaller fragments can represent up to seventy percent of the total cell free DNA in the maternal blood sample.{{citation needed|date=February 2022}}

===Analysis of cffDNA===
In real-time PCR, fluorescent probes are used to monitor the accumulation of [[amplicon]]s. The reporter fluorescent signal is proportional to the number of amplicons generated. The most appropriate real time PCR protocol is designed according to the particular mutation or genotype to be detected. Point mutations are analysed with qualitative real time PCR with the use of [[allele]] specific probes. [[Insertion (genetics)|Insertions]] and [[deletion (genetics)|deletions]] are analyzed by dosage measurements using quantitative real time PCR.{{citation needed|date=February 2024}}

cffDNA may be detected by finding paternally inherited DNA sequences via [[polymerase chain reaction]] (PCR).<ref name=Traeger-Synodinos2006>{{cite journal | vauthors = Traeger-Synodinos J | title = Real-time PCR for prenatal and preimplantation genetic diagnosis of monogenic diseases | journal = Molecular Aspects of Medicine | volume = 27 | issue = 2–3 | pages = 176–91 | year = 2006 | pmid = 16430951 | doi = 10.1016/j.mam.2005.12.004 | publisher = Elsevier BV }}</ref><ref name=Boon2007>{{cite journal | vauthors = Boon EM, Schlecht HB, Martin P, Daniels G, Vossen RH, den Dunnen JT, Bakker B, Elles R | title = Y chromosome detection by Real Time PCR and pyrophosphorolysis-activated polymerisation using free fetal DNA isolated from maternal plasma | journal = Prenatal Diagnosis | volume = 27 | issue = 10 | pages = 932–7 | date = October 2007 | pmid = 17600849 | doi = 10.1002/pd.1804 | publisher = Wiley-Blackwell | s2cid = 24498216 }}</ref>

====Quantitative real-time PCR====
[[Testis-determining factor|Sex-determining region Y]] gene (SRY) and [[Y-STR|Y chromosome short tandem repeat]] "DYS14" in cffDNA from 511 pregnancies were analyzed using quantitative real-time PCR (RT-qPCR). In 401 of 403 pregnancies where maternal blood was drawn at seven weeks gestation or more, both segments of DNA were found.<ref name=Hill2010>{{cite journal | vauthors = Hill M, Pařízek A, Cibula D, Kancheva R, Jirásek JE, Jirkovská M, Velíková M, Kubátová J, Klímková M, Pašková A, Zižka Z, Kancheva L, Kazihnitková H, Zamrazilová L, Stárka L | title = Steroid metabolome in fetal and maternal body fluids in human late pregnancy | journal = The Journal of Steroid Biochemistry and Molecular Biology | volume = 122 | issue = 4 | pages = 114–32 | date = October 2010 | pmid = 20580824 | doi = 10.1016/j.jsbmb.2010.05.007 | publisher = Elsevier BV | s2cid = 25820012 }}</ref>

====Nested PCR====
The use of [[nested polymerase chain reaction]] (nested PCR) was evaluated to determine sex by detecting a Y chromosome specific signal in the cffDNA from maternal plasma. Nested PCR detected 53 of 55 male fetuses. The cffDNA from the plasma of 3 of 25 women with female fetuses contained the Y chromosome-specific signal. The [[sensitivity and specificity|sensitivity]] of nested PCR in this experiment was 96 percent. The [[sensitivity and specificity|specificity]] was 88 percent.<ref name=Al-Yatama2001>{{cite journal | vauthors = Al-Yatama MK, Mustafa AS, Ali S, Abraham S, Khan Z, Khaja N | title = Detection of Y chromosome-specific DNA in the plasma and urine of pregnant women using nested polymerase chain reaction | journal = Prenatal Diagnosis | volume = 21 | issue = 5 | pages = 399–402 | date = May 2001 | pmid = 11360283 | doi = 10.1002/pd.69 | publisher = Wiley-Blackwell | s2cid = 20169086 }}</ref>

====Digital PCR====
[[Microfluidic|Microfluidic devices]] allow the quantification of cffDNA segments in maternal plasma with accuracy beyond that of real-time PCR. [[Point mutation]]s, loss of [[zygosity|heterozygosity]] and [[aneuploidy]] can be detected in a single PCR step.<ref name=Zimmermann2008>{{cite journal | vauthors = Zimmermann BG, Grill S, Holzgreve W, Zhong XY, Jackson LG, Hahn S | s2cid = 2909830 | title = Digital PCR: a powerful new tool for noninvasive prenatal diagnosis? | journal = Prenatal Diagnosis | volume = 28 | issue = 12 | pages = 1087–93 | date = December 2008 | pmid = 19003785 | doi = 10.1002/pd.2150 | publisher = Wiley-Blackwell | doi-access = free }}</ref><ref name=Lo2007/><ref name=Quake2007>{{cite journal | vauthors = Quake S | title = At the interface of physics and biology | journal = BioTechniques | volume = 43 | issue = 1 | page = 19 | date = July 2007 | doi = 10.2144/000112501 | pmid = 17695250 | doi-access = free }}</ref> Digital PCR can differentiate between maternal blood plasma and fetal DNA in a [[Multiplex polymerase chain reaction|multiplex]] fashion.<ref name=Zimmermann2008/>

====Shotgun sequencing====
High throughput [[shotgun sequencing]] using tools such as Solexa or Illumina yields approximately 5 million [[Sequence-tagged site|sequence tags]] per sample of maternal serum. Aneuploid pregnancies such as [[trisomy]] were identified when testing at the fourteenth week of gestation. Fetal [[whole genome sequencing|whole of genome mapping]] by parental [[haplotype]] analysis was completed using sequencing of cffDNA from maternal serum.<ref name=Lo2008/> Pregnant females were studied using a 2-plex massively parallel maternal plasma DNA sequencing and trisomy was diagnosed with z-score greater than 3.<ref name=ChiuLo2010>{{cite journal | vauthors = Chiu RW, Lo YM | title = Pregnancy-associated microRNAs in maternal plasma: a channel for fetal-maternal communication? | journal = Clinical Chemistry | volume = 56 | issue = 11 | pages = 1656–7 | date = November 2010 | pmid = 20837782 | doi = 10.1373/clinchem.2010.153684 | publisher = American Association for Clinical Chemistry (AACC) | doi-access = free }}</ref> The sequencing gave sensitivity of 100 percent, specificity of 97.9 percent, a [[positive predictive value]] of 96.6 percent and a [[negative predictive value]] of 100 percent.{{citation needed|date=February 2024}}

====Mass spectrometry====
[[Matrix-assisted laser desorption/ionization]]-[[time-of-flight mass spectrometry]] (MALDI-TOF MS) combined with [[single-base extension]] after PCR allows cffDNA detection with single base specificity and single DNA molecule sensitivity.<ref name=Ding2008>{{cite book | vauthors = Ding C | title = Prenatal Diagnosis | chapter = MALDI-TOF Mass Spectrometry for Analyzing Cell-Free Fetal DNA in Maternal Plasma | volume = 444 | pages = 253–67 | year = 2008 | pmid = 18425487 | doi = 10.1007/978-1-59745-066-9_20 | publisher = Humana Press | isbn = 978-1-58829-803-4 | location = Totowa, NJ | series = Methods in Molecular Biology }}</ref> DNA is amplified by PCR. Then, linear [[amplification (molecular biology)|amplification]] with base extension reaction (with a third primer) is designed to [[annealing (biology)|anneal]] to the region upstream from the [[mutation]] site. One or two [[nucleobase|bases]] are added to the extension primer to produce two extension products from wild-type DNA and mutant DNA. Single base specificity provides advantages over hybridization-based techniques using [[TaqMan]] hydrolysis probes. When assessing the technique, no false positives or negatives were found when looking for cffDNA to determine fetal sex in sixteen maternal plasma samples.<ref name=Ding2008/> The sex of ninety-one male foetuses were correctly detected using MALDI-TOF mass spectrometry. The technique had accuracy, sensitivity and specificity of over 99 percent.<ref name=AkolekarFarkas2010>{{cite journal | vauthors = Akolekar R, Farkas DH, VanAgtmael AL, Bombard AT, Nicolaides KH | s2cid = 20744999 | title = Fetal sex determination using circulating cell-free fetal DNA (ccffDNA) at 11 to 13 weeks of gestation | journal = Prenatal Diagnosis | volume = 30 | issue = 10 | pages = 918–23 | date = October 2010 | pmid = 20721878 | doi = 10.1002/pd.2582 | publisher = Wiley-Blackwell }}</ref>

====Epigenetic modifications====
Differences in gene activation between maternal and fetal DNA can be exploited. [[Epigenetics|Epigenetic modifications]] (heritable modifications that change gene function without changing DNA sequence) can be used to detect cffDNA.<ref name=TongChiu2012>{{cite journal | vauthors = Tong YK, Chiu RW, Chan KC, Leung TY, Lo YM | title = Technical concerns about immunoprecipitation of methylated fetal DNA for noninvasive trisomy 21 diagnosis | journal = Nature Medicine | volume = 18 | issue = 9 | pages = 1327–8; author reply 1328–9 | date = September 2012 | pmid = 22961155 | doi = 10.1038/nm.2915 | publisher = Springer Nature | s2cid = 31316176 }}</ref><ref name=Papageorgiou2011>{{cite journal | vauthors = Papageorgiou EA, Karagrigoriou A, Tsaliki E, Velissariou V, Carter NP, Patsalis PC | title = Fetal-specific DNA methylation ratio permits noninvasive prenatal diagnosis of trisomy 21 | journal = Nature Medicine | volume = 17 | issue = 4 | pages = 510–3 | date = April 2011 | pmid = 21378977 | pmc = 3977039 | doi = 10.1038/nm.2312 | publisher = Springer Nature }}</ref> The [[Methylation|hypermethylated]] [[RASSF1|RASSF1A]] promoter is a universal fetal marker used to confirm the presence of cffDNA.<ref name=WhiteDent2012>{{cite journal | vauthors = White HE, Dent CL, Hall VJ, Crolla JA, Chitty LS | title = Evaluation of a novel assay for detection of the fetal marker RASSF1A: facilitating improved diagnostic reliability of noninvasive prenatal diagnosis | journal = PLOS ONE | volume = 7 | issue = 9 | article-number = e45073 | date = 14 September 2012 | pmid = 23024794 | pmc = 3443218 | doi = 10.1371/journal.pone.0045073 | publisher = Public Library of Science (PLoS) | editor-first = Cees | editor-last = Oudejans | bibcode = 2012PLoSO...745073W | doi-access = free }}</ref> A technique was described where cffDNA was extracted from maternal plasma and then digested with methylation-sensitive and insensitive [[restriction enzyme]]s. Then, real-time PCR analysis of RASSF1A, SRY, and DYS14 was done.<ref name=WhiteDent2012/> The procedure detected 79 out of 90 (88 percent) maternal blood samples where hypermethylated RASSF1A was present.{{citation needed|date=February 2024}}

====mRNA====
mRNA transcripts from genes expressed in the placenta are detectable in maternal plasma.<ref name=Ng2002>{{cite journal | vauthors = Ng EK, Tsui NB, Lam NY, Chiu RW, Yu SC, Wong SC, Lo ES, Rainer TH, Johnson PJ, Lo YM | title = Presence of filterable and nonfilterable mRNA in the plasma of cancer patients and healthy individuals | journal = Clinical Chemistry | volume = 48 | issue = 8 | pages = 1212–7 | date = August 2002 | pmid = 12142376 | doi = 10.1093/clinchem/48.8.1212 | doi-access = free }}</ref> In this procedure, plasma is centrifuged so an aqueous layer appears. This layer is transferred and from it [[RNA]] is extracted. [[RT-PCR]] is used to detect a selected expression of RNA. For example, [[Human placental lactogen]] (hPL) and [[beta-hCG]] mRNA are stable in maternal plasma and can be detected. (Ng et al. 2002). This can help to confirm the presence of cffDNA in maternal plasma.<ref name=WrightBurton2009/>

==Applications==
===Prenatal sex discernment===
{{Further|Prenatal sex discernment}}
The analysis of cffDNA from a sample of maternal plasma allows for [[prenatal sex discernment]]. Applications of prenatal sex discernment include:
* '''Disease testing''': Whether the sex of the fetus is male or female allows the determination of the risk of a particular [[sex linkage|X-linked recessive genetic disorder]] in a particular pregnancy, especially where the mother is a [[genetic carrier]] of the disorder.<ref name=BairdAnderson1988>{{cite journal | vauthors = Baird PA, Anderson TW, Newcombe HB, Lowry RB | title = Genetic disorders in children and young adults: a population study | journal = American Journal of Human Genetics | volume = 42 | issue = 5 | pages = 677–93 | date = May 1988 | pmid = 3358420 | pmc = 1715177 }}</ref>
* '''Preparation''', for any sex-dependent aspects of parenting.{{citation needed|date=February 2024}}
* '''[[Sex selection]]''', which after preimplantation genetic diagnosis may be performed by selecting only embryos of the preferred sex, or, after post-implantation methods by performing [[sex-selective abortion]] depending on the test result and personal preference.

In comparison to [[obstetric ultrasonography]] which is unreliable for sex determination in the first trimester and amniocentesis which carries a small risk of [[miscarriage]], sampling of maternal plasma for analysis of cffDNA is without risk.<ref name=Scheffer2010>{{cite journal | vauthors = Scheffer PG, van der Schoot CE, Page-Christiaens GC, Bossers B, van Erp F, de Haas M | title = Reliability of fetal sex determination using maternal plasma | journal = Obstetrics and Gynecology | volume = 115 | issue = 1 | pages = 117–26 | date = January 2010 | pmid = 20027043 | doi = 10.1097/aog.0b013e3181c3c938 | publisher = Ovid Technologies (Wolters Kluwer Health) | s2cid = 26126381 }}</ref> The main targets in the cffDNA analysis are the gene responsible for the sex-determining region Y protein (SRY) on the [[Y chromosome]] and the DYS14 sequence.<ref name=Bustamante-Aragones2010>{{cite journal | vauthors = Bustamante-Aragones A, Gonzalez-Gonzalez C, de Alba MR, Ainse E, Ramos C | title = Noninvasive prenatal diagnosis using ccffDNA in maternal blood: state of the art | journal = Expert Review of Molecular Diagnostics | volume = 10 | issue = 2 | pages = 197–205 | date = March 2010 | pmid = 20214538 | doi = 10.1586/erm.09.86 | publisher = Informa UK Limited | s2cid = 207219250 }}</ref><ref name=ZimmermannEl-Sheikhah2005>{{cite journal | vauthors = Zimmermann B, El-Sheikhah A, Nicolaides K, Holzgreve W, Hahn S | title = Optimized real-time quantitative PCR measurement of male fetal DNA in maternal plasma | journal = Clinical Chemistry | volume = 51 | issue = 9 | pages = 1598–604 | date = September 2005 | pmid = 16020496 | doi = 10.1373/clinchem.2005.051235 | publisher = American Association for Clinical Chemistry (AACC) | doi-access = free }}</ref>

===Congenital adrenal hyperplasia===
In [[congenital adrenal hyperplasia]], the [[adrenal cortex]] lacks appropriate [[corticosteroid]] synthesis, leading to excess adrenal androgens and affects female fetuses.<ref name=FinningChitty2008>{{cite journal | vauthors = Finning KM, Chitty LS | title = Non-invasive fetal sex determination: impact on clinical practice | journal = Seminars in Fetal & Neonatal Medicine | volume = 13 | issue = 2 | pages = 69–75 | date = April 2008 | pmid = 18243829 | doi = 10.1016/j.siny.2007.12.007 | publisher = Elsevier BV }}</ref> There is an external masculinization of the genitalia in the female fetuses.<ref name=MarkeyWadia2005>{{cite journal | vauthors = Markey CM, Wadia PR, Rubin BS, Sonnenschein C, Soto AM | title = Long-term effects of fetal exposure to low doses of the xenoestrogen bisphenol-A in the female mouse genital tract | journal = Biology of Reproduction | volume = 72 | issue = 6 | pages = 1344–51 | date = June 2005 | pmid = 15689538 | doi = 10.1095/biolreprod.104.036301 | publisher = Oxford University Press (OUP) | doi-access = free }}</ref> Mothers of at risk fetuses are given [[dexamethasone]] at 6 weeks gestation to suppress [[pituitary gland]] release of [[androgen]]s.<ref name=SayresCho2011>{{cite journal | vauthors = Sayres LC, Cho MK | s2cid = 17018886 | title = Cell-free fetal nucleic acid testing: a review of the technology and its applications | journal = Obstetrical & Gynecological Survey | volume = 66 | issue = 7 | pages = 431–42 | date = July 2011 | pmid = 21944155 | doi = 10.1097/ogx.0b013e31822dfbe2 | publisher = Ovid Technologies (Wolters Kluwer Health) }}</ref>

If analysis of cffDNA obtained from a sample of maternal plasma lacks genetic markers found only on the Y chromosome, it is suggestive of a female fetus. However, it might also indicate a failure of the analysis itself (a false negative result). Paternal [[genetic polymorphisms]] and sex-independent markers may be used to detect cffDNA. A high degree of heterozygosity of these markers must be present for this application.<ref name=HillBarrett2012>{{cite journal | vauthors = Hill M, Barrett AN, White H, Chitty LS | title = Uses of cell free fetal DNA in maternal circulation | journal = Best Practice & Research. Clinical Obstetrics & Gynaecology | volume = 26 | issue = 5 | pages = 639–54 | date = October 2012 | pmid = 22542961 | doi = 10.1016/j.bpobgyn.2012.03.004 | publisher = Elsevier BV }}</ref>

===Paternity testing===
Prenatal [[DNA paternity testing]] is commercially available. The test can be performed at nine weeks gestation.{{citation needed|date=December 2017}}

===Single gene disorders===
[[dominance (genetics)|Autosomal dominant and recessive]] single gene disorders which have been diagnosed prenatally by analysing paternally inherited DNA include [[cystic fibrosis]], [[beta thalassemia]], [[sickle cell anemia]], [[spinal muscular atrophy]], and [[myotonic dystrophy]].<ref name=Traeger-Synodinos2006/><ref name=Bustamante-Aragones2010/> Prenatal diagnosis of single gene disorders which are due to an autosomal recessive mutation, a maternally inherited autosomal dominant mutation or large sequence mutations that include duplication, expansion or insertion of DNA sequences is more difficult.<ref name=NorburyNorbury2008>{{cite journal | vauthors = Norbury G, Norbury CJ | title = Non-invasive prenatal diagnosis of single gene disorders: how close are we? | journal = Seminars in Fetal & Neonatal Medicine | volume = 13 | issue = 2 | pages = 76–83 | date = April 2008 | pmid = 18234572 | doi = 10.1016/j.siny.2007.12.008 | publisher = Elsevier BV }}</ref>

In cffDNA, fragments of 200 {{ndash}} 300 bp length involved in single gene disorders are more difficult to detect.{{citation needed|date=February 2022}}

For example, the autosomal dominant condition, [[achondroplasia]] is caused by the FGFR3 gene point mutation.<ref name=LiPage-Christiaens2007>{{cite journal | vauthors = Li Y, Page-Christiaens GC, Gille JJ, Holzgreve W, Hahn S | title = Non-invasive prenatal detection of achondroplasia in size-fractionated cell-free DNA by MALDI-TOF MS assay | journal = Prenatal Diagnosis | volume = 27 | issue = 1 | pages = 11–7 | date = January 2007 | pmid = 17154237 | doi = 10.1002/pd.1608 | publisher = Wiley-Blackwell | s2cid = 5808436 }}</ref> In two pregnancies with a fetus with achondroplasia was found a paternally inherited G1138A mutation from cffDNA from a maternal plasma sample in one and a G1138A de novo mutation from the other.<ref name=LiPage-Christiaens2007/>

In studies of the genetics of [[Huntington's chorea]] using qRT-PCR of cffDNA from maternal plasma samples, [[Trinucleotide repeat disorder|CAG repeats]] have been detected at normal levels (17, 20 and 24).<ref name="Die-Smulders2013">[https://archive.today/20130616012452/http://humupd.oxfordjournals.org/content/19/3/304] {{cite journal |vauthors=de Die-Smulders CE, de Wert GM, Liebaers I, Tibben A, Evers-Kiebooms G |year=2013 |title=Reproductive options for prospective parents in families with Huntington's disease: clinical, psychological and ethical reflections |journal=Human Reproduction Update |volume=19 |issue=3 |pages=304–15 |doi=10.1093/humupd/dms058 |pmid=23377865 |doi-access=free}}</ref>

cffDNA may also be used to diagnose [[genetic disorder|single gene disorders]].<ref name=HahnChitty2008>{{cite journal | vauthors = Hahn S, Chitty LS | title = Noninvasive prenatal diagnosis: current practice and future perspectives | journal = Current Opinion in Obstetrics & Gynecology | volume = 20 | issue = 2 | pages = 146–51 | date = April 2008 | pmid = 18388814 | doi = 10.1097/GCO.0b013e3282f73349 | s2cid = 7222299 }}</ref> Developments in laboratory processes using cffDNA may allow [[prenatal testing|prenatal diagnosis]] of [[aneuploidy|aneuploidies]] such as [[trisomy 21]] (Down syndrome) in the fetus.<ref name=FanBlumenfeld2008>{{cite journal | vauthors = Fan HC, Blumenfeld YJ, Chitkara U, Hudgins L, Quake SR | title = Noninvasive diagnosis of fetal aneuploidy by shotgun sequencing DNA from maternal blood | journal = Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America | volume = 105 | issue = 42 | pages = 16266–71 | date = October 2008 | pmid = 18838674 | pmc = 2562413 | doi = 10.1073/pnas.0808319105 | publisher = Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences | bibcode = 2008PNAS..10516266F | doi-access = free }}</ref><ref name=Lo2007>{{cite journal | vauthors = Lo YM, Lun FM, Chan KC, Tsui NB, Chong KC, Lau TK, Leung TY, Zee BC, Cantor CR, Chiu RW | title = Digital PCR for the molecular detection of fetal chromosomal aneuploidy | journal = Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America | volume = 104 | issue = 32 | pages = 13116–21 | date = August 2007 | pmid = 17664418 | pmc = 1934923 | doi = 10.1073/pnas.0705765104 | publisher = Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences | doi-access = free | bibcode = 2007PNAS..10413116L }}</ref>

===Hemolytic disease of the fetus and newborn===
Incompatibility of fetal and maternal [[Rh blood group system|RhD antigens]] is the main cause of [[Hemolytic disease of the newborn]].<ref name="Cardo 2010">{{cite journal | vauthors = Cardo L, García BP, Alvarez FV | title = Non-invasive fetal RHD genotyping in the first trimester of pregnancy | journal = Clinical Chemistry and Laboratory Medicine | volume = 48 | issue = 8 | pages = 1121–6 | date = August 2010 | pmid = 20482298 | doi = 10.1515/cclm.2010.234 | publisher = Walter de Gruyter GmbH | s2cid = 31027958 | hdl = 10651/7879 | hdl-access = free }}</ref> Approximately 15 percent of [[Caucasian race|Caucasian]] women, 3 to 5 percent of black [[Africa]] women and less than 3 percent of [[Asia]]n women are RhD negative.<ref name="Chinen2010">{{cite journal | vauthors = Chinen PA, Nardozza LM, Martinhago CD, Camano L, Daher S, Pares DB, Minett T, Araujo Júnior E, Moron AF | title = Noninvasive determination of fetal rh blood group, D antigen status by cell-free DNA analysis in maternal plasma: experience in a Brazilian population | journal = American Journal of Perinatology | volume = 27 | issue = 10 | pages = 759–62 | date = November 2010 | pmid = 20408112 | doi = 10.1055/s-0030-1253560 | publisher = Georg Thieme Verlag KG | s2cid = 25705372 }}</ref>

Accurate prenatal diagnosis is important because the disease can be fatal to the newborn and because treatment including intramuscular [[immunoglobulin]] (Anti-D) or intravenous [[immunoglobulin]] can be administered to mothers at risk.<ref name="Okwundu2013">{{cite journal | vauthors = Okwundu CI, Afolabi BB | title = Intramuscular versus intravenous anti-D for preventing Rhesus alloimmunization during pregnancy | journal = The Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews | issue = 1 | article-number = CD007885 | date = January 2013 | pmid = 23440818 | doi = 10.1002/14651858.CD007885.pub2 | pmc = 11694612 }}</ref>

PCR to detect [[RHD (gene)]] gene [[exon]]s 5 and 7 from cffDNA obtained from maternal plasma between 9 and 13 weeks gestation gives a high degree of specificity, sensitivity and diagnostic accuracy (>90 percent) when compared to RhD determination from newborn [[cord blood]] serum.<ref name="Cardo 2010"/> Similar results were obtained targeting exons 7 and 10.<ref name="Aykut2013">{{cite journal | vauthors = Aykut A, Onay H, Sagol S, Gunduz C, Ozkinay F, Cogulu O | title = Determination of fetal rhesus d status by maternal plasma DNA analysis | journal = Balkan Journal of Medical Genetics | volume = 16 | issue = 2 | pages = 33–8 | date = December 2013 | pmid = 24778561 | pmc = 4001413 | doi = 10.2478/bjmg-2013-0029 | publisher = Walter de Gruyter GmbH }}</ref> Droplet digital PCR in fetal RhD determination was comparable to a routine real-time PCR technique.<ref name="Svobodová_2015">{{cite journal | vauthors = Svobodová I, Pazourková E, Hořínek A, Novotná M, Calda P, Korabečná M | title = Performance of Droplet Digital PCR in Non-Invasive Fetal RHD Genotyping - Comparison with a Routine Real-Time PCR Based Approach | journal = PLOS ONE | volume = 10 | issue = 11 | article-number = e0142572 | date = 2015 | pmid = 26562517 | pmc = 4642940 | doi = 10.1371/journal.pone.0142572 | bibcode = 2015PLoSO..1042572S | doi-access = free }}</ref>

Routine determination of fetal RhD status from cffDNA in maternal serum allows early management of at risk pregnancies while decreasing unnecessary use of Anti-D by over 25 percent.<ref name="Papasavva2016">{{cite journal | vauthors = Papasavva T, Martin P, Legler TJ, Liasides M, Anastasiou G, Christofides A, Christodoulou T, Demetriou S, Kerimis P, Kontos C, Leontiades G, Papapetrou D, Patroclos T, Phylaktou M, Zottis N, Karitzie E, Pavlou E, Kountouris P, Veldhuisen B, van der Schoot E, Kleanthous M | title = Prevalence of RhD status and clinical application of non-invasive prenatal determination of fetal RHD in maternal plasma: a 5 year experience in Cyprus | journal = BMC Research Notes | volume = 9 | issue = 1 | page = 198 | date = April 2016 | pmid = 27036548 | pmc = 4818414 | doi = 10.1186/s13104-016-2002-x | publisher = Springer Nature | doi-access = free }}</ref>

===Aneuploidy===
;Sex chromosomes
Analysis of maternal serum cffDNA by high-throughput sequencing can detect common fetal [[sex chromosome]] [[aneuploidies]] such as [[Turner's syndrome]], [[Klinefelter's syndrome]] and [[triple X syndrome]] but the procedure's [[positive predictive value]] is low.<ref name="Zhang2017">{{cite journal | vauthors = Zhang B, Lu BY, Yu B, Zheng FX, Zhou Q, Chen YP, Zhang XQ | title = Noninvasive prenatal screening for fetal common sex chromosome aneuploidies from maternal blood | journal = The Journal of International Medical Research | volume = 45 | issue = 2 | pages = 621–630 | date = April 2017 | pmid = 28357876 | pmc = 5536640 | doi = 10.1177/0300060517695008 | publisher = SAGE Publications }}</ref>
[[File:Prenatal Down syndrome screening algorithm.png|thumb|An example of an algorithm for determining the indication for prenatal genetic testing for trisomy 21 ([[Down syndrome]]), wherein the ''genetic blood test'' (in center) is performed by detecting cffDNA in a blood sample from the mother.<ref>Diagram by Mikael Häggström, MD, using following source: {{cite web|url=https://www.uptodate.com/contents/should-i-have-a-screening-test-for-down-syndrome-during-pregnancy-beyond-the-basics/print|title=Patient education: Should I have a screening test for Down syndrome during pregnancy? (Beyond the Basics)|website=UpToDate|author=Jacquelyn V Halliday, MSGeralyn M Messerlian, PhDGlenn E Palomaki, PhD}} This topic last updated: Feb 16, 2023.</ref>]]
;Trisomy 21
Fetal trisomy of [[chromosome 21]] is the cause of Down syndrome. This trisomy can be detected by analysis of cffDNA from maternal blood by massively parallel shotgun sequencing (MPSS).<ref name= "Kazemi 2016">{{cite journal | vauthors = Kazemi M, Salehi M, Kheirollahi M | title = Down Syndrome: Current Status, Challenges and Future Perspectives | journal = International Journal of Molecular and Cellular Medicine | volume = 5 | issue = 3 | pages = 125–133 | date = 10 August 2016 | pmid = 27942498 | pmc = 5125364 }}</ref> Another technique is digital analysis of selected regions (DANSR).<ref name="Kazemi 2016"/> Such tests show a sensitivity of about 99% and a specificity of more than 99.9%. Therefore, they cannot be regarded as diagnostic procedures but may be used to confirm a positive maternal screening test such as a first trimester screening or ultrasound markers of the condition.<ref name="Kazemi 2016"/><ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Mersy E, Smits LJ, van Winden LA, de Die-Smulders CE, Paulussen AD, Macville MV, Coumans AB, Frints SG | title = Noninvasive detection of fetal trisomy 21: systematic review and report of quality and outcomes of diagnostic accuracy studies performed between 1997 and 2012 | journal = Human Reproduction Update | volume = 19 | issue = 4 | pages = 318–29 | year = 2013 | pmid = 23396607 | doi = 10.1093/humupd/dmt001 | doi-access = free }}</ref>

;Trisomy 13 and 18
Analysis of cffDNA from maternal plasma with MPSS looking for trisomy 13 or 18 is possible<ref name="Clark-Ganheart2014">{{cite journal | vauthors = Clark-Ganheart CA, Iqbal SN, Brown DL, Black S, Fries MH | title = Understanding the Limitations of Circulating Cell Free Fetal DNA: An Example of Two Unique Cases | journal = Journal of Clinical Gynecology and Obstetrics | volume = 3 | issue = 2 | pages = 38–70 | date = May 2014 | pmid = 25298847 | pmc = 4185925 | doi = 10.14740/jcgo229w }}</ref>

Factors limiting sensitivity and specificity include the levels of cffDNA in the maternal plasma; maternal chromosomes may have [[mosaicism]].<ref name=Wataganara2003>{{cite journal | vauthors = Wataganara T, LeShane ES, Farina A, Messerlian GM, Lee T, Canick JA, Bianchi DW | title = Maternal serum cell-free fetal DNA levels are increased in cases of trisomy 13 but not trisomy 18 | journal = Human Genetics | volume = 112 | issue = 2 | pages = 204–8 | date = February 2003 | pmid = 12522563 | doi = 10.1007/s00439-002-0853-9 | s2cid = 9721963 }}</ref>

A number of fetal [[nucleic acid]] molecules derived from aneuploid chromosomes can be detected including SERPINEB2 mRNA, clad B, hypomethylated SERPINB5 from [[chromosome 18]], placenta-specific 4 (PLAC4), hypermethylated holocarboxylase synthetase (HLCS) and c21orf105 mRNA from [[chromosome 12]].<ref name=ChiuLo2011>{{cite journal | vauthors = Chiu RW, Lo YM | title = Non-invasive prenatal diagnosis by fetal nucleic acid analysis in maternal plasma: the coming of age | journal = Seminars in Fetal & Neonatal Medicine | volume = 16 | issue = 2 | pages = 88–93 | date = April 2011 | pmid = 21075065 | doi = 10.1016/j.siny.2010.10.003 | publisher = Elsevier BV }}</ref> With complete trisomy, the mRNA alleles in maternal plasma isn't the normal 1:1 ratio, but is in fact 2:1. Allelic ratios determined by epigenetic markers can also be used to detect the complete trisomies. Massive parallel sequencing and digital PCR for fetal aneuploidy detection can be used without restriction to fetal-specific nucleic acid molecules.  (MPSS) is estimated to have a [[sensitivity and specificity|sensitivity]] of between 96 and 100%, and a [[sensitivity and specificity|specificity]] between 94 and 100% for detecting Down syndrome. It can be performed at 10 weeks of [[Gestational age (obstetrics)|gestational age]].<ref name=oxhp>[https://www.oxhp.com/secure/policy/noninvasive_prenatal_diagnosis_fetal_aneuploidy.pdf Noninvasive Prenatal Diagnosis of Fetal Aneuploidy Using Cell-Free Fetal Nucleic Acids in Maternal Blood: Clinical Policy (Effective 05/01/2013)] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140307093626/https://www.oxhp.com/secure/policy/noninvasive_prenatal_diagnosis_fetal_aneuploidy.pdf |date=2014-03-07 }} from Oxford Health Plans</ref> One study in the United States estimated a [[false positive]] rate of 0.3% and a [[positive predictive value]] of 80% when using cffDNA to detect Down syndrome.<ref name=Bianchi2014>{{cite journal | vauthors = Bianchi DW, Parker RL, Wentworth J, Madankumar R, Saffer C, Das AF, Craig JA, Chudova DI, Devers PL, Jones KW, Oliver K, Rava RP, Sehnert AJ | s2cid = 13278444 | title = DNA sequencing versus standard prenatal aneuploidy screening | journal = The New England Journal of Medicine | volume = 370 | issue = 9 | pages = 799–808 | date = February 2014 | pmid = 24571752 | doi = 10.1056/NEJMoa1311037 | doi-access = free }}. A recent study in the [http://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa1407349?#t=article New England Journal of Medicine] demonstrated the feasibility of using [http://www.ariosadx.com/ NIPT] in a low risk population.</ref>

===Preeclampsia===
[[Preeclampsia]] is a complex condition of pregnancy involving [[hypertension]] and [[proteinuria]] usually after 20 weeks gestation.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Henderson JT, Thompson JH, Burda BU, Cantor A | title = Preeclampsia Screening: Evidence Report and Systematic Review for the US Preventive Services Task Force | journal = JAMA | volume = 317 | issue = 16 | pages = 1668–1683 | date = April 2017 | pmid = 28444285 | doi = 10.1001/jama.2016.18315 | publisher = American Medical Association (AMA) | s2cid = 205077025 }}</ref> It is associated with poor [[cytotrophoblast]]ic invasion of the [[myometrium]]. Onset of the condition between 20 and 34 weeks gestation, is considered "early".<ref name="Seval 2015">{{cite journal | vauthors = Seval MM, Karabulut HG, Tükün A, Koç A | title = Cell free fetal DNA in the plasma of pregnant women with preeclampsia | journal = Clinical and Experimental Obstetrics & Gynecology | volume = 42 | issue = 6 | pages = 787–91 | year = 2015 | doi = 10.12891/ceog1982.2015 | pmid = 26753487 | s2cid = 20971322 | doi-access = free }}</ref> Maternal plasma samples in pregnancies complicated by preeclampsia have significantly higher levels of cffDNA that those in normal pregnancies.<ref name=Lo1999c>{{cite journal | vauthors = Lo YM, Lau TK, Zhang J, Leung TN, Chang AM, Hjelm NM, Elmes RS, Bianchi DW | title = Increased fetal DNA concentrations in the plasma of pregnant women carrying fetuses with trisomy 21 | journal = Clinical Chemistry | volume = 45 | issue = 10 | pages = 1747–51 | date = October 1999 | doi = 10.1093/clinchem/45.10.1747 | pmid = 10508120 | doi-access = free }}</ref><ref name=LeungZhang2001>{{cite journal | vauthors = Leung TN, Zhang J, Lau TK, Chan LY, Lo YM | title = Increased maternal plasma fetal DNA concentrations in women who eventually develop preeclampsia | journal = Clinical Chemistry | volume = 47 | issue = 1 | pages = 137–9 | date = January 2001 | pmid = 11148193 | doi = 10.1093/clinchem/47.1.137 | doi-access = free }}</ref><ref name=ZhongHolzgreve2002>{{cite journal | vauthors = Zhong XY, Holzgreve W, Hahn S | title = The levels of circulatory cell free fetal DNA in maternal plasma are elevated prior to the onset of preeclampsia | journal = Hypertension in Pregnancy | volume = 21 | issue = 1 | pages = 77–83 | year = 2002 | pmid = 12044339 | doi = 10.1081/prg-120002911 | publisher = Informa UK Limited | s2cid = 72519129 }}</ref> This holds true for early onset preeclampsia.<ref name="Seval 2015"/>

== History ==
In 1997, Hong Kong molecular biologist [[Dennis Lo]] and his team first employed the Y-PCR assay to identify fetal Y chromosome sequences (because Y-specific sequences are genetic sequences of the fetus not in the maternal genome<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Ramezanzadeh |first1=Mahboubeh |last2=Khosravi |first2=Sharifeh |last3=Salehi |first3=Rasoul |date=2017 |title=Cell-free Fetal Nucleic Acid Identifier Markers in Maternal Circulation |journal=Advanced Biomedical Research |language=en |volume=6 |issue=1 |page=89 |doi=10.4103/2277-9175.211800 |doi-access=free |issn=2277-9175 |pmc=5549546 |pmid=28828340}}</ref>) in maternal plasma samples.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Lo |first1=Y M Dennis |last2=Corbetta |first2=Noemi |last3=Chamberlain |first3=Paul F |last4=Rai |first4=Vik |last5=Sargent |first5=Ian L |last6=Redman |first6=Christopher WG |last7=Wainscoat |first7=James S |date=1997-08-16 |title=Presence of fetal DNA in maternal plasma and serum |url=https://linkinghub.elsevier.com/retrieve/pii/S0140673697021740 |journal=The Lancet |language=en |volume=350 |issue=9076 |pages=485–487 |doi=10.1016/S0140-6736(97)02174-0|pmid=9274585 |url-access=subscription }}</ref> For this groundbreaking work, Lo was honored with the 2022 Lasker DeBakey Clinical Medical Research Award.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Hofschneider |first=Mark |title=Noninvasive prenatal testing using fetal DNA |url=https://laskerfoundation.org/winners/noninvasive-prenatal-testing-using-fetal-dna/ |access-date=2024-05-06 |website=Lasker Foundation |language=en-US}}</ref>

==Future perspectives==
[[DNA sequencing|New generation sequencing]] may be used to yield a [[whole genome sequencing|whole genome sequence]] from cffDNA. This raises ethical questions.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Yurkiewicz IR, Korf BR, Lehmann LS | s2cid = 205109276 | title = Prenatal whole-genome sequencing--is the quest to know a fetus's future ethical? | journal = The New England Journal of Medicine | volume = 370 | issue = 3 | pages = 195–7 | date = January 2014 | pmid = 24428465 | doi = 10.1056/NEJMp1215536 }}</ref> However, the utility of the procedure may increase as clear associations between specific genetic variants and disease states are discovered.<ref name="pmid17554300">{{cite journal | author = Wellcome Trust Case Control Consortium | title = Genome-wide association study of 14,000 cases of seven common diseases and 3,000 shared controls | journal = Nature | volume = 447 | issue = 7145 | pages = 661–78 | date = June 2007 | pmid = 17554300 | pmc = 2719288 | doi = 10.1038/nature05911 | bibcode = 2007Natur.447..661B }}</ref><ref name="pmid17898773">{{cite journal | vauthors = Mailman MD, Feolo M, Jin Y, Kimura M, Tryka K, Bagoutdinov R, Hao L, Kiang A, Paschall J, Phan L, Popova N, Pretel S, Ziyabari L, Lee M, Shao Y, Wang ZY, Sirotkin K, Ward M, Kholodov M, Zbicz K, Beck J, Kimelman M, Shevelev S, Preuss D, Yaschenko E, Graeff A, Ostell J, Sherry ST | display-authors = 6 | title = The NCBI dbGaP database of genotypes and phenotypes | journal = Nature Genetics | volume = 39 | issue = 10 | pages = 1181–6 | date = October 2007 | pmid = 17898773 | pmc = 2031016 | doi = 10.1038/ng1007-1181 }}</ref>

extract: Cell-free fetal DNA (cffDNA) is fetal DNA that circulates freely in the maternal blood. Maternal blood is sampled by venipuncture. Analysis of cffDNA is a method of non-invasive prenatal diagnosis frequently ordered for pregnant women of advanced age. Two hours after delivery, cffDNA is no longer detectable in maternal blood.
